newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian police raid mosque, say seeking weapons.
newsitem.headline: Russian police raid mosque, say seeking weapons.

text.p: Russian anti-riot police beat up worshippers as they prayed in a Moscow mosque and herded them off for interrogation with a "most cynical" disregard for their religious feelings, a Moslem organisation said on Wednesday.
Police said in a statement that they had carried out a search for weapons after being asked by a Moslem official to remove three people who were disturbing the other worshippers.
Nine of the worshippers, who included ethnic Chechens and Ingushis from southern Russia, were arrested in the Tuesday evening raid but later released, the statement said.

"Around 1900 (1500 GMT) a group of armed people in camouflage entered the Historical Mosque without explanation and started to beat and drag away worshippers," said the Union of Moslems of Russia in a press statement.

"This was the cruellest, most cynical insult to believers' feelings," it said, adding that the police, from the interior ministry's crack OMON squad, had used bad language and had beaten some worshippers inside the mosque.

The Union of Moslems said that once on a bus outside the mosque, the police forced worshippers onto their knees and told them: "You will now spend the rest of your lives bowing not only to Allah but to the Moscow OMON", the Union said.
The police statement said that only one man who had entered the building had removed his shoes in accordance with Moslem tradition while the riot police waited outside.
Of the nine arrested, seven were found to have problems with their identification documents, said the statement, carried by Itar-Tass news agency.

Interfax news agency earlier quoted an unnamed police source as saying the raid was part of a clampdown on crime and that a majority of those detained did not have proper documents for living in Moscow.
"Criminal elements constantly circle the mosque, which complicates the situation in the centre of the city," Interfax quoted the official as saying.

Russian officials, including representatives of the Security Council and the Russian Orthodox Church, were expected to visit the mosque later on Wednesday to discuss the incident, the Union's statement said.
Russia has had a policy of religious tolerance since the collapse of the atheistic Soviet Union in 1991 but remains nervous about the influence of Islam, especially in its southern regions.
Its army waged a bloody 21-month campaign against separatists in predominantly-Moslem Chechnya, where a delicate ceasefire now prevails.

Moscow authorities periodically round up darker skinned people believed to be from Chechnya and other Caucasus regions whom they suspect of being heavily involved in organised crime or of being domiciled in the capital illegally.
